answer.answer:
The single cited route to improving site safety is prefabrication and off-site work: moving the work into a factory takes people out of the hazardous zone, and it is the only such path in the record, backed by peer-reviewed evidence and exhibited by 12 of the 50 coded cases. Making that route work is mostly an organisational job rather than a purchase: it needs design for manufacture and assembly, early contractor involvement, an integrated supply chain and precise up-front planning, and none of those four is a machine. Separately, where people and robots do share the site, collaborative operation held within power and force limits reduces contact injury risk, and that in turn requires workforce training and compliance with robot safety standards. Watch the gap between claim and mechanism: 39 of the 50 cases claim the safety benefit, while only 12 carry the prefabrication path that explains it.

**The one cited path into site safety**

VA13 "Improve site safety" (Value) carries exactly 1 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, and 39 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] That single inbound edge is DEP19: PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site" (Process) enablesCapability VA13 "Improve site safety", peer-reviewed, carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases, on the ground that moving work offsite improves site safety [1]. Because the dependency lookup is exact and lists every edge touching VA13, this can be stated as a total: prefabrication is the only asserted producer of site safety in the graph, and the other 27 cases that draw on VA13 do so without carrying that edge. 20 of the 50 coded cases draw on PR2 itself. [1] VA13 applies in the Structural Construction phase, in a value-realizing role [2].

**What prefabrication itself requires**

PR2 carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges [1]. Its upstream requirements are, in order of how many cases carry the edge:

- DEP15: PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" enablesCapability PR2, peer-reviewed, carried by 15 of the 50 cases, since DfMA orients the project toward offsite manufacture [1]; 15 of the 50 cases draw on PR9 [1].
- DEP22: CO11 "Early contractor involvement" (Condition) enablesCapability PR2, carried by 13 of the 50 cases: integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase [1]; 14 of the 50 cases draw on CO11 [1].
- DEP79: VA14 "Integrate supply chain" enablesCapability PR2, carried by 12 of the 50 cases, supply chain integration supporting the offsite production line [1]; 14 of the 50 cases draw on VA14 [1].
- DEP33: PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning" (Risk), carried by 18 of the 50 cases: prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1]; 36 of the 50 cases draw on RI14 [1], an order of magnitude above the 1-case enablers elsewhere in this retrieval and by far the most widely held of these conditions.
- DEP96: PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", carried by 10 of the 50 cases, a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requiring third-party certification and traceability [1].

None of these five is a Resource: they are a Process, a Condition, a Value and two Risks. The safety gain is bought with delivery-model and planning work, not with equipment. Alongside safety, PR2 also yields VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" (19 of 50 carry the edge) [1], VA3 "Improve quality/performance" (18 of 50) [1] and VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" (14 of 50) [1]. Note also that PR4 "Robotic assembly" hasPrecondition PR2 (DEP55, carried by 4 of the 50 cases): automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [1], so prefabrication sits upstream of robotic assembly as well as upstream of safety.

**The second, distinct route: safety of the shared workspace**

This one lands on a different node, RI20 "Work safety concern", not on VA13, so it should not be reported as a path to site safety. DEP57: CO6 "Human-robot interaction" (Condition) mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern", evidence grade standard, carried by 4 of the 50 coded cases, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigating contact-injury risk [1]. 32 of the 50 cases draw on CO6 [1], but only 4 carry that mitigation. Its own preconditions are DEP34: CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", peer-reviewed, carried by 27 of the 50 cases, because the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1], and DEP45: CO6 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", evidence grade standard, carried by 2 of the 50 cases, human-robot collaborative work depending on compliance with robot safety standards [1]. 44 of the 50 cases draw on RI6 [1], so the training requirement is near-universal while the standards-compliance edge is carried by 2.

**The robot hardware itself carries no safety edge**

RE2 "Robotic arm" carries 1 inbound and 1 outbound edge and is drawn on by 22 of the 50 cases [1]; both edges run to and from PR4 "Robotic assembly" (DEP24 [1], DEP11 [1]), not to safety. RE15 "Unmanned mobile vehicle" is drawn on by 25 of the 50 cases and carries no dependency edges at all. [1] Their link to safety in this material is statistical only: Improve site safety (VA13) co-occurs with Human-robot interaction (CO6) at weight 28 and Unmanned mobile vehicle (RE15) with CO6 at weight 23 [3], and VA13 co-occurs with Robotic pickup/selection (PR15) at weight 18 [4]. Co-occurrence is correlation across cases, not a directional claim, and these lists are ranked cuts (120 co-occurring enablers in total for PR15 [4]), so nothing about absence can be read from them. One caution worth carrying into route planning: DEP44: RI5 "Location dependent/site constraint" constrains PR12 "Path-planning", carried by 15 of the 50 cases, since reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors [1].

**Deployed record**

Three deployed processes in the context were adopted for safety reasons. census_RXM4-5 was adopted to address safety and labor, performs digging and material handling on sitework, substructure and foundation, at technology readiness level 8. [5] census_RXM1-3 was adopted to address safety and market, performs digging and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8. [6] census_RXM23-1 was adopted to address safety, performs drilling on the structural core and sitework, at technology readiness level 7. [7] All three remove people from digging, handling or drilling work rather than from the site as a whole, which is the substitution route, not the prefabrication route. The context gives no firm for any of the three, and it does not link any of them to VA13, PR2 or CO6, so none can be said to exhibit those enablers; the evidence that prefabrication delivers site safety rests here on the literature edge and its 12 carrying cases, not on a named deployed project.
